cim: The End of Man: The real danger isn’t artificial intelligence
cim_eredeti: The End of Man: The real danger isn’t artificial intelligence
szoveg_eredeti:
First came a massive Microsoft outage. Then a nationwide ground stop that disrupted thousands of flights. Then major banks experienced problems with their online systems. Then United Airlines grounded departing flights. Then reports that the highly classified network that the National Security Agency uses for its internal communications had gone down. Then Apple joined the growing list of technology giants experiencing widespread disruptions.

One breakdown after another. Millions of Americans reminded just how dependent their daily lives have become on technologies they neither understand nor control.

This is what happens when technology goes haywire.

Whether the culprit is artificial intelligence, cyberattackers, outdated equipment, poor planning, inadequate maintenance, or human error, the larger problem remains.

Who is responsible when the technological systems upon which society depends begin to fail?

We’ve been asking the wrong question about artificial intelligence.

Maybe the real danger isn’t that machines might become smarter than human beings.

Maybe it’s the human hunger for power—and our willingness to surrender control to those who wield it.

Hollywood has spent decades warning us about machines that might someday become so intelligent, so independent and so powerful that they no longer need human beings.

In Stanley Kubrick’s “2001: A Space Odyssey,” the seemingly infallible computer HAL 9000 turns against the astronauts who have entrusted their lives to its control.

Yet the more unsettling vision may come from an unlikely source: Pixar’s animated children’s film “WALL-E.” In “WALL-E,” humanity has abandoned an uninhabitable Earth and retreated to a massive spaceship where nearly every human need is anticipated and satisfied by machines.

People no longer walk. They no longer work. They barely notice the world around them. They have become passive consumers of their own existence.

In “2001,” the nightmare is a machine that refuses to surrender control. In “WALL-E,” the nightmare is a humanity that has forgotten how to exercise it. Both films arrive at a troubling truth: technology becomes dangerous when human beings cease to exercise meaningful control over it.

And therein lies the problem: we have confused technological progress with human progress.

From the atomic bomb to computers, the internet and surveillance cameras, technologies developed for one purpose have repeatedly been turned into instruments of destruction and control.

And now artificial intelligence threatens to magnify all of these capabilities, allowing governments, corporations and criminals to monitor, manipulate and control human behavior on an unprecedented scale.

The technology may be new, but the human impulses driving its misuse are as old as civilization itself.

Consider the FBI’s latest warning about ARTEX, an artificial-intelligence tool originally developed to help cybersecurity professionals identify weaknesses in computer networks.

In the hands of cybercriminals, that same technology has become a weapon.

Meanwhile, Google’s Threat Intelligence Group warns that malicious actors are increasingly deploying autonomous AI systems capable of identifying vulnerabilities and carrying out attacks at machine speed, with dramatically reduced human intervention.

The machines didn’t suddenly develop criminal intentions. Human beings created the tools, identified the targets and put the systems to work.

Artificial intelligence has not eliminated human greed, arrogance or the lust for power. It has given those impulses greater reach, greater speed and greater power.

And we especially cannot afford to ignore those who wield these technologies in the name of government.

But computers can be wrong. Algorithms can be biased. Databases can contain errors. Automated systems can perpetuate and magnify the mistakes, prejudices and political agendas of those who build and operate them.

The government does not acquire a constitutional exemption merely because its abuses are carried out by a computer rather than a human being. Indeed, the more powerful the technology, the greater the need for meaningful restraints on the people who control it.

Fifty years ago, the Senate’s Church Committee exposed extensive abuses by America’s intelligence agencies, including surveillance operations directed against citizens exercising their constitutional rights.

The warning was unmistakable: government power, particularly when exercised secretly and without effective oversight, can become a direct threat to the freedoms it is supposed to protect.

Yet the constitutional questions remain the same.

Who watches the watchers? Who holds the government accountable when it uses technology to circumvent the constitutional restraints meant to keep its power in check?

Forty years ago, in 1986, I explored many of these concerns in my book “The End of Man.”

The concern was not simply that computers might someday become powerful enough to dominate society. It was that human beings themselves were increasingly being reduced to systems of information, objects to be classified, studied, managed and manipulated.

As I warned then, “Man is not a machine.”

This is precisely why the Constitution matters.

The Bill of Rights was written for a world in which human beings, entrusted with power, could not always be trusted to exercise that power responsibly.

Greed remains greed. Arrogance remains arrogance. And tyranny does not become less dangerous simply because it is administered by an algorithm.

In “The End of Man,” I also contemplated a future in which humanity’s technological creations might become so powerful that they would presume to take the place of God. I wrote:

If all goes according to plan for the AI people, one can imagine and expect a “metallic” future. It might go something like this: In some lonely outpost in the distant future where all the computers in the universe are linked together, some foreboding human servant asks, “Is there a God?” Striking the questioner down for his impudence, the computers reply, “Now there is.”

Fast-forward to 2021, when Mo Gawdat, a former Google executive, warned of the extraordinary power of artificial intelligence: “The reality is we’re creating God.”

Yet perhaps the greater danger isn’t that machines will become gods.

Forty years after “The End of Man,” the question confronting humanity is not simply how intelligent our machines will become. It is how much of our own humanity we are willing to surrender in the pursuit of technological progress.

The greatest danger may not come from a machine that learns to think like a human being.

It may come from human beings who stop thinking, stop questioning, stop resisting and stop taking responsibility for the world they are creating.

In the end, the machines may not be what brings about the end of man.

John W. Whitehead is founder and president of The Rutherford Institute. Nisha Whitehead is the Executive Director of The Rutherford Institute. Information about The Rutherford Institute is available at www.rutherford.org.
